analysis.one_liner: Bans forced arbitration agreements in Medicare and Medicaid nursing homes and home care.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have let nursing home residents and home care patients sue in court instead of being forced into private arbitration, was introduced in April 2024 and died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Nursing homes and home care providers often require residents and patients to sign agreements, at or before admission, saying any future dispute will be settled by a private arbitrator rather than a judge and jury. This bill would make those pre-dispute arbitration agreements unenforceable for anyone receiving Medicare skilled nursing care, Medicaid nursing home care, Medicaid home- and community-based services, or home health care. A resident who was neglected or injured could then take the facility to court, and existing agreements would no longer be valid.
analysis.who_benefits: Nursing home residents and people receiving Medicaid-funded home care, along with their families. These are often frail, elderly, or disabled people who signed admission paperwork without bargaining power. The bill would preserve their right to a public trial with a jury, public court records, and the possibility of damages large enough to deter neglect and abuse.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nursing home residents and home care patients

how_it_helps.text: The bill bars skilled nursing facilities and nursing facilities from requiring, accepting, or enforcing pre-dispute arbitration agreements with residents, and declares any such agreement invalid, including ones already signed. [S3]
The same prohibition covers providers of Medicaid home- and community-based services and home health care services, including their employees, agents, and affiliates. [S3]
Questions about whether the ban applies to a particular agreement would be decided by a court under federal law, not by the arbitrator the facility chose. [S3]

The CRS summary states the bill prohibits and nullifies existing pre-dispute arbitration agreements for Medicare and Medicaid nursing facilities, home- and community-based services, and home health care. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Nursing home chains and home care providers, which would lose their ability to keep disputes out of court, and the arbitration industry that administers these cases. Facilities argue jury verdicts for neglect or abuse can be far larger than arbitration awards, and some of that cost could be passed on through higher prices, though federal programs cover most nursing home care.
analysis.who_pays_short: Nursing home chains and home care providers

drawbacks.text: Supporters of arbitration argue it can resolve disputes faster and at lower cost than litigation, and this bill leaves residents no option to choose arbitration after a dispute arises, even voluntarily. [S3]

Nursing homes could face larger jury awards for neglect and abuse claims; facilities largely paid through Medicare and Medicaid might seek higher reimbursement rates or cut costs elsewhere to absorb the added liability. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is concrete for a vulnerable group: someone harmed by neglect in a nursing home or by a home care aide keeps access to a courtroom, where proceedings are public and verdicts can reflect the full harm. The costs fall on the provider side, and some could show up as higher service prices or more defensive practices. Most nursing home care is paid by Medicare and Medicaid, so the public already bears much of the facilities' cost structure; the bill shifts dispute resolution away from a private system the facility picks toward an open one.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Blumenthal, joined by Senator Hirono, introduced the bill on April 9, 2024. [S1]
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day. [S5]
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nursing home chains and home care providers keep the ability to route neglect and abuse disputes into private arbitration, and residents remain bound by agreements signed at admission.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nursing home chains keep forced arbitration

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban pre-dispute arbitration agreements in Medicare and Medicaid nursing facilities and home care.

for.name: Sen. Mazie Hirono
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsor.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever happened; both sponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on, but no one is recorded opposing it either.

industries.note: These facilities routinely use arbitration agreements signed at admission to keep neglect and abuse claims out of court, where awards and publicity are larger. The bill would have stripped that protection, exposing them to jury trials.

industries.industry: Home care and home- and community-based services providers
industries.note: Medicaid-funded home care agencies and their affiliates could no longer enforce arbitration agreements against the people they serve, opening their disputes to court as well.
Private arbitration firms would lose the stream of nursing home and home care disputes the bill covers, and the bill ensures courts rather than arbitrators decide threshold questions.
